metadata.title: Gradient Descent: Steps Go Against the Gradient
metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.objective: Let a learner who knows algebra but not calculus see why a step goes opposite the gradient.
metadata.learner: Knows basic algebra; has not studied calculus.
misconceptions: A larger learning rate is always better
expectedUnderstanding: The gradient of f(x)=x^2 is 2x, which points toward increasing f, that is, uphill.
The update x - eta*(2x) moves opposite the gradient, toward the valley at x=0.
The learning rate eta scales how far the step goes, and a step larger than half the valley width crosses over instead of settling.

primitives.text: Gradient descent: each step goes against the gradient
green: step = -eta * gradient, which points downhill
eta below 0.5 stops before the valley; above 0.5 it overshoots

controls.label: Drag the point along the curve

checkpoints.title: A point on a cost curve
checkpoints.body: The blue dot sits at position x on f(x) = x^2. The curve is a cost we want to make small, and the bottom of the valley is at x = 0.

checkpoints.title: Which way does the gradient point?
checkpoints.body: Predict: the gradient here is 2x. On the right of the valley it points right, toward higher f. Is that uphill or downhill? Say your answer, then continue.

checkpoints.title: Turn it around
checkpoints.body: The update is x - eta*(2x). The green arrow is the red gradient reversed and scaled by eta, so it points downhill toward the valley. The gradient itself points uphill.

checkpoints.title: Step size is a trade-off
checkpoints.body: Raise eta past 0.5 and the green step lands on the far side of the valley. Near eta = 1 the point flips side to side instead of settling. A larger learning rate is not automatically better.

checkpoints.title: Try it yourself
checkpoints.body: Set eta near 0.2 and drag x from 2 down to 0. Watch the green arrow shrink as the slope flattens, and watch the hollow green dot land closer to the valley.

narration.text: Here is a cost curve, f of x equals x squared. The blue point is our current guess.
The slope at that point is 2x. Taken as a direction, the gradient points toward bigger cost, which is uphill.
Because the gradient points uphill, the update subtracts it. That minus sign is the whole idea.
Now the step: x minus eta times 2x. Eta sets how far along the downhill direction we travel.
Push eta past one half and the step crosses the valley. Near eta equals one, the point just flips side to side.

fallback.text: Static figure. A parabola f(x) = x^2 with a blue point at x on the curve and a drop line to the x-axis. A red arrow along the axis points in the +2x direction, which is uphill. A green arrow from the same start points in the -2x direction, scaled by eta, which is the step. A hollow green dot marks the next position x - 2*eta*x on the curve. With eta above 0.5 the next dot lands on the far side of the valley at x = 0.

accessibility.alt: A parabola f(x)=x squared with a movable point. A red arrow shows the gradient +2x pointing uphill; a green arrow shows the step -eta*2x pointing downhill and scaled by the learning rate eta; a hollow green dot shows where the next step lands, crossing the valley at x=0 when eta is above 0.5.
